title: Navigation: LAG, LEAD & Neighbors
objective: After this lesson you will be able to compare each row with its neighbors using LAG/LEAD (offsets, defaults, partitions), fetch endpoints with FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE (with correct framing), and express deltas and streaks without self-joins.
why: Rankings order rows; navigation *relates* them — hour gaps between consecutive learners, progress jumps between enrollments, first-vs-current comparisons. Pre-window SQL did this with self-joins on row numbers (fragile, slow); navigation functions read neighbors directly in one pass. Month-over-month reports are LAG queries wearing business clothes.

blocks.text: **`LAG(col, offset, default)`** reads a previous row's value; **`LEAD`** reads ahead — within the partition, along the ORDER BY. Defaults handle edges (first row has no previous: `LAG(x, 1, 0)` yields 0 instead of NULL). Offsets beyond 1 compare across gaps (week-over-week-same-weekday needs offset 7 thinking, applied to daily series).

blocks.code:
-- Hour gaps between consecutively-ranked developers (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, hours_studied,
  LAG(hours_studied, 1) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS prev_hours,
  hours_studied - LAG(hours_studied, 1, hours_studied) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS gap_below
FROM developers
ORDER BY hours_studied DESC;
blocks.caption: LAG with a self-default: first row gaps to zero instead of NULL

blocks.text: The default trick (`hours_studied` as its own default) makes edge arithmetic clean: first row's gap computes to 0, not NULL — no COALESCE wrapper needed downstream. Choose defaults deliberately per column (0 for measures, '' for text, endpoint values for bounded series).

**`FIRST_VALUE`** returns the partition's first row value; **`LAST_VALUE`** returns the *frame's* last — and the default growing frame makes LAST_VALUE mean 'last so far', i.e. the current row, almost never what you want. The fix is the explicit full-partition frame (`ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`) — LAST_VALUE's most famous bug, worth memorizing as a pair.

blocks.code:
-- First vs last hours per role: FIRST works by luck, LAST needs the frame
-- (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT DISTINCT role,
  FIRST_VALUE(hours_studied) OVER w AS top_hours,
  LAST_VALUE(hours_studied) OVER w AS bottom_hours_WRONG,
  LAST_VALUE(hours_studied) OVER (
    PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS bottom_hours
FROM developers
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied DESC);
blocks.caption: LAST_VALUE without a full frame returns 'last so far' — usually the current row

blocks.text: Two bonuses in one query: the **WINDOW clause** names a window definition once (`WINDOW w AS (…)`) and reuses it — DRY for multi-function queries (supported in SQLite and PostgreSQL). And `SELECT DISTINCT` collapses the per-row repetition when you only want one row per partition — the standard endpoint-summary shape.

Neighbor arithmetic replaces whole classes of self-joins: deltas (`x - LAG(x)`), changes (`LAG` comparison for flip detection), running extrema (`MAX(x) OVER (ORDER BY t)` as peak-so-far). Each is one ordered pass instead of a join plus dedupe — simpler plans, simpler reading, no pair-dedupe predicates.

blocks.query: SELECT name, hours_studied FROM developers ORDER BY hours_studied DESC LIMIT 5;
blocks.note: Run this ordered top-5 in the sandbox — it is the sequence LAG/LEAD walk. Read adjacent pairs and compute one gap by hand: that hand computation is exactly what the neighbor functions automate, and verifying it grounds every query in this lesson.

items: LAG/LEAD read neighbors along ORDER BY within partitions; offsets + defaults handle edges and gaps
LAST_VALUE needs an explicit full-partition frame — default growing frames make it 'last so far'
WINDOW clause names definitions once (SQLite + PG); DISTINCT collapses endpoint summaries
Deltas, flips, and running extrema replace self-join patterns in one ordered pass

exercise.prompt: (a) In the sandbox, run the ordered top-5 and hand-compute two adjacent gaps. (b) In real SQLite/PostgreSQL, write: (i) full ordered list with prev_hours and gap_below (self-defaulted); (ii) per-role top and bottom hours using FIRST_VALUE + framed LAST_VALUE with a named WINDOW; (iii) developers whose hours exceed the previous developer's by 100+ (gap filter outside). (c) State why (iii) needs the outer query.
hints: Hand gaps first — e.g., 947→912 = 35. Your LAG query must reproduce these exact numbers; mismatch means wrong ORDER BY.
(ii) needs PARTITION BY role + ORDER BY hours DESC, one named WINDOW reused by both functions, and the explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame on LAST_VALUE only.
(iii) filters on a window alias → pipeline order (Ch.1): compute inside, filter outside. Gap >= 100 on gap_below.
exercise.solution:
-- (b-i) gaps (real SQLite / PostgreSQL)
SELECT name, hours_studied,
  hours_studied - LAG(hours_studied, 1, hours_studied) OVER (ORDER BY hours_studied DESC) AS gap_below
FROM developers ORDER BY hours_studied DESC;
-- (b-ii) endpoints with named window
SELECT DISTINCT role,
  FIRST_VALUE(hours_studied) OVER w AS top_hours,
  LAST_VALUE(hours_studied) OVER (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS bottom_hours
FROM developers WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied DESC);
-- (b-iii) big jumpers: wrap (i), filter gap_below >= 100 outside.
exercise.why: Hand computation first makes the functions checkable, not magical; the framed LAST_VALUE fixes the lesson's signature bug by construction; the outer filter rehearses pipeline order for the third time — repetition across lessons is how staging rules stick.

quiz.q: LAG(hours, 1) on the first ordered row returns?
options: NULL (no previous row) unless a default is given
quiz.explain: Edges have no neighbors: LAG/LEAD yield NULL past the boundary. Defaults (LAG(x, 1, 0)) make edge arithmetic clean — choose per column.

quiz.q: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (PARTITION BY r ORDER BY h DESC) returns the current row's value on every row. Why?
options: Default growing frame: 'last of peers-so-far' is the current row — add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
quiz.explain: ORDER BY flips the default frame to running prefix, so LAST_VALUE sees only rows up to current. The explicit full frame is the mandatory pairing — memorize them together.

quiz.q: What does WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours DESC) buy you?
options: Names the definition once for reuse across functions — DRY multi-function queries (SQLite + PG)
Nothing — syntax sugar that changes semantics
quiz.explain: Same semantics, single definition: FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, RANK over identical windows without repetition drift. Repeat the definition thrice and they will diverge during maintenance.

quiz.q: Filtering gap_below >= 100 must wrap the LAG query. Why?
options: Pipeline: windows evaluate after WHERE — the alias doesn't exist at filter time
quiz.explain: Same staging rule as ranks (Ch.1–2): compute inside, filter outside. WHERE predates windows in every engine.

summary: Neighbors overtake self-joins: LAG/LEAD with offsets and defaults, FIRST/LAST with mandatory framing, WINDOW naming, DISTINCT summaries. Deltas and streaks become one ordered pass — and filters still wrap outside.
next: Neighbors compare points — frames aggregate spans. Next: frame mastery (ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS, moving averages, exclusion) and the running-total subtleties this course opened with.
